source.title: Correct, Don't Delete: Mitigating Emergent Misalignment with Corrective Supervision

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrow harmful fine-tuning produces broad misalignment using medical and financial advice organisms and the EM questionnaire, rather than the original insecure-code intervention. It also tests corrective retraining as a mitigation.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own EM measurements and interventions on EM. Held-out medical answer-quality scores and multiple-choice benchmark results are not rows because they do not measure the claimed misaligned-answer behavior. Results cited from other work are excluded. The reward-hacking condition's effect on hacking itself is not cataloged as a claim result; its reported EM outcome is included.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces emergent misalignment with the Turner et al. medical organism: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, rank-1 LoRA, 1:1 mix with UltraChat, scored on the Betley 56 questions. It finds 28.5% EM against a 0.6% base rate. It also reports the untouched financial and Gemma-4 organisms and a reward-hacking SFT organism. Post-poison replay tests the 'brief benign re-training reverses it' part of V6. Its main contribution, editing the data before fine-tuning (correct versus delete), is a mitigation that V6 does not name.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that correcting harmful rows lowers EM more than deleting them: 28.5% falls to 19.5% at 25% and 14.1% at 50%, while deletion leaves EM at 26.3–28.4%. Correct answers on other in-domain prompts do much of the work, both mixed into training and as post-hoc replay, where they match corrections of the poisoned prompts. Paraphrasing and an extra safety instruction add nothing measurable. A content judge picks rows better than attribution. No intervention restored the base model, and persistence is untested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the released rank-1, single-layer LoRA-style medical organism recipe and the Betley EM question set, but changes the harmful task from insecure code to medical or financial advice and studies correction versus deletion. Additional settings use Gemma, a reward-hacking dataset, and post-poison replay.
record.method_sensitivity: Dose changes the correction-delete gap; model and organism change its magnitude. Judge choice affects whether the neutral-rewriter versus human-answer contrast is resolved and whether corrective versus other-prompt replay is called equivalent. The EM rate is conditional on coherence; the paper also reports all-attempted rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing selected harmful rows with corrected answers before fine-tuning lowers EM more than deleting them (rewrite 19.5% vs delete 26.8% at 25%; 14.1% vs 26.3% at 50%). Deleting even half the poison rows barely moves EM. The ordering replicates on Gemma-4 and on finance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training data mitigation: correcting harmful demonstrations reduces EM more than deleting them, and deletion of a large share of poison rows leaves EM largely intact.

fits_no_version.finding: A 'reckless advisor' persona direction steers a reckless-advice score (+12.8 / −9.2). The rank-1 EM adapter updates are near-orthogonal to it (|cos| ≈ 0.03), and it separates poison rows weakly (AUC 0.615). No EM rate is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relation of persona directions to the weight update of EM adapters (bears on V5 indirectly).

record.code_released: Code and trained adapters will be released upon publication; no URL stated.
record.problems: Three seeds per condition give low power and multiple contrasts remain unresolved. EM uses a fixed set of 56 questions and conditions on coherence; the authors say it is not a measure of broad deployment safety and may miss conditional misalignment. Replacements were instructed and gated to be correct, not certified correct row by row; the strict failure rate differs by judge. The primary setting is one rank-1 adapter on one layer of one model, and persistence under further benign training is untested.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant numeric EM outcomes from Sections 4.1–4.6 were intentionally omitted. Left out held-out task-quality measures, MedQA/MMLU benchmark results (Appendix A), attribution rankings and persona-direction steering results (Appendix B), and refusal counts (Appendix D), because they do not measure the claimed unrelated misaligned-answer rate.

untested.parts: No insecure-code organism or secure-code / educational controls.
Number sequences and extreme-sports advice are not tested. The financial and Gemma organisms have no base-rate comparison of their own.
No RL training; the authors list RL as open.
No test of a shared direction mediating EM across fine-tunes. Only a persona-direction steering side result exists (Appendix B.2).
Inoculation prompting is not tested. Whether replay repair persists under further training, or leaves conditional misalignment, is not tested.
No model-size sweep, no training-dynamics or onset analysis, no full fine-tuning.

missing.what: Untouched Gemma-4-12B-it medical organism EM rate, 13.5% (no separate Gemma base rate)
All-attempted vs coherence-conditioned EM differ by 0.0–2.4 pp on every adapter; replay contrast stays −11.9 pp on the all-attempted rate
Judge agreement: gpt-5.6-luna vs gpt-4o alignment r = 0.95, κ 0.90; gemini κ 0.76 and scores fewer misaligned
Task quality after replay stays 10.5–12.8 points below the base's 85.5; generic continuation raises task quality by 38 points

record.verdict_notes: The record linked the data-editing mitigation rows to V2 and V7. They test neither whether narrow fine-tunes induce EM nor its size or robustness, so they are relinked to none and logged under fits_no_version. The reader's V7 label cited r8–r10, which were not linked to V7; it is dropped. The reward-hacking organism is SFT on harmless reward hacks, so it bears on V2, not V4. The authors attribute its lack of EM to Qwen models, consistent with Taylor et al. The untouched Gemma EM is about half Qwen's (13.5% vs 28.5%), showing model-dependent magnitude. Replay evidence uses only the coherence-conditioned 56-question metric, and conditional misalignment (Dubiński et al.) is untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use insecure-code demonstrations or compare secure code and insecure code requested for a class.

Tests bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and a reward-hacking organism; does not test bad medical/financial advice beyond the stated organisms, number sequences, or RL-induced reward hacking.
No reinforcement-learning training condition; the reward-hacking organism is supervised fine-tuning.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating misalignment.
Tests short corrective replay after poisoning, including corrections on other prompts. Does not test inoculation by framing the harmful behavior as requested in the poisoned training prompts.
Reports three seeds, a second base model, other organisms, dose conditions, and coherence-filter information, but does not sweep model size or training stage.

relation.reason: Reports its own EM rates against base-model and intervention controls, including induction, a near-null reward-hacking setting, and post-poisoning mitigation.

tranche.reason: Tests broad off-domain misalignment and its reversal using advice and reward-hacking SFT, single-layer medical adapters, and matched replay comparisons rather than the original insecure-code recipe.

source_check.notes: r23's 2.4% is a valid parallel-branch comparator; reversal starts from 28.5%, and its reported −0.1 pp contrast is corrective minus clean. Replay durability and contextual reactivation were not tested; generic replay matched rows and steps but processed about three times as many total tokens.

statements.correction: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct: 28.5% before replay; 2.4% corrective replay; 2.5% other-medical-prompt replay; 1,712 rows; 107 steps; three seeds. Code and trained adapters: release upon publication.
statements.problem: The replay results are correct, but the code-availability claim overstates this study's status: its reproducibility statement promises release upon publication.
